title: Disaster recovery and multi-region
scopeHtml: Scope: RPO/RTO, DR strategies, active-passive vs active-active, replication and PITR, failover, drills, multi-region data. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: Disaster recovery basics: RPO and RTO
notes.html:
Disaster recovery (DR) is the plan to get a system working again after a big failure: a datacenter loss, region outage, data corruption, ransomware or a human mistake.

Two numbers define the plan:

  • RPO (Recovery Point Objective): how much data you can afford to lose, measured in time. RPO = 15 minutes means after recovery you may lose the last 15 minutes of writes. RPO = 0 means no loss, which needs synchronous replication.
  • RTO (Recovery Time Objective): how long you can be down. RTO = 1 hour means service restored within an hour.
        last good copy        disaster              service back
 ---------|---------------------|---------------------|--------->
          <------- RPO -------->|<-------- RTO ------->
          (data you lose)         (downtime you suffer)

Lower RPO and RTO cost more, roughly 10x per step. Business decides the numbers per system: a bank ledger might need RPO 0 and RTO minutes; an internal analytics dashboard can accept RPO 24 h and RTO 1 day.

Also distinguish:

  • High availability (HA): survive component failures automatically within a site/region (seconds to minutes).
  • DR: survive loss of the whole site or region, often with a human decision.
  • Backups: protect against corruption and deletion, which replication does NOT (it copies the bad delete everywhere).

Worked example. Payments service: RPO 0, RTO 5 min. Needs synchronous replication across zones (RPO 0 within region) plus a tested automatic failover. Reports service: RPO 24 h, RTO 8 h. A nightly snapshot copied to another region is enough, costing a few dollars per month.

Industry examples. AWS Well-Architected lists the four DR strategies (backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, multi-site active-active); Amazon S3 offers 11 nines of durability but customers still enable versioning because deletion by mistake is not covered by durability; GitLab's 2017 incident deleted production data and then found 4 of 5 backup methods were not working.

Everyday analogy. RPO is how many pages of your essay you can afford to lose if the laptop dies; RTO is how long you can go without a working computer before the deadline.

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing RPO and RTO.
  • Saying replication replaces backups.
  • Setting RPO/RTO without discussing cost, or without business input.

notes.title: The four DR strategies
notes.html:
From cheapest and slowest to most expensive and fastest (the AWS framing):

Strategy RPO RTO Cost What runs in the DR region
Backup and restore Hours Hours to a day Lowest Nothing, only backups
Pilot light Minutes Tens of minutes Low Data replicated; core infra defined but off or minimal
Warm standby Seconds to minutes Minutes Medium Full stack at reduced capacity, running
Active-active (multi-site) Near 0 Near 0 (seconds) Highest Full stack serving real traffic

Backup and restore. Snapshots and WAL archives stored in another region. Recovery means creating infrastructure from code (Terraform) then restoring data; restore time depends on data size: 10 TB at 1 GB/s effective is still about 3 hours before verification.

Pilot light. Database replicated continuously; app servers exist as images/templates but are scaled to zero. On disaster scale them up and flip DNS.

Warm standby. A small but complete copy runs constantly (say 20% capacity). On failover autoscale to 100%. Fast, but must be validated: untested standby capacity limits cause failed failovers.

Worked example. Service costs 100K USD/month. Backup/restore adds about 2%, pilot light 10 to 15%, warm standby 30 to 50%, active-active 100%+ (plus complexity in data). Pick by the cost of downtime: if an hour of outage costs 500K USD, active-active may pay for itself with one avoided incident per year.

Decision gravity. The strategy is a business decision that shapes data architecture. Upgrading from pilot light to active-active later requires redesigning data replication and conflict handling: practically a one-way door, so decide the target early even if you start cheaper.

Industry examples. Netflix is active-active across AWS regions (evacuates a failing region in minutes using traffic steering); many banks use warm standby; startups usually start with backup/restore and cross-region snapshots.

Everyday analogy. Spare keys: one in a drawer at home (backup), a friend with a key and a bed made up (warm standby), or two flats you live in half the week (active-active).

Common interview traps.

  • Jumping to active-active for everything.
  • Not accounting for data size when promising an RTO.
  • Forgetting that DR also needs secrets, DNS, certificates, and IAM in the second region.

notes.title: Active-passive vs active-active
notes.html:
Active-passive: one region serves traffic; the other is on standby and takes over on failure. Active-active: both (all) regions serve traffic at the same time.

Active-passive Active-active
Writes Single primary region Writes accepted in many regions
Failover Promote standby, flip traffic Remove failed region from routing
User latency Far users pay cross-region RTT Users hit the nearest region
Complexity Moderate High (conflicts, global uniqueness)
Wasted capacity Standby mostly idle None, but need headroom to absorb a lost region

The hard part is data. Active-active needs a strategy for concurrent writes:

  • Partition users by home region (geo-sharding): each user's data has one "home" write region; other regions only read or proxy. No conflicts, simple, but a failover moves ownership. Uber, Slack and many B2C apps do this.
  • Multi-leader replication with conflict resolution: LWW, CRDTs, application merge. DynamoDB global tables use last-writer-wins with timestamps; Cassandra multi-DC with LOCAL_QUORUM; CockroachDB/Spanner use consensus across regions (strong consistency, cross-region write latency of 50 to 150 ms).
  • Single write region, read replicas elsewhere: reads are local, writes pay the trip (Aurora Global Database: one writer region, replication typically under 1 second lag, cross-region failover/promotion takes about a minute in AWS docs; confirm).

Capacity math. With 2 active regions, to survive losing one, each must handle 100% of traffic: 2x provisioned, utilization capped at 50%. With 3 regions, each normally takes 1/3 of traffic; if one dies, each survivor takes 1/2, i.e. 1.5x its usual load, so each can run at up to 66% utilisation. More regions make N+1 cheaper.

Industry examples. Netflix (active-active, multi-region Cassandra); Amazon retail; Google Spanner (multi-region consensus); Facebook (regional with home-region data and TAO); Booking.com. DynamoDB global tables and Aurora Global DB are managed options.

Decision gravity. Active-passive is a modest, mostly reversible step. Active-active is a deep architectural commitment: you must design for it (idempotency, conflict handling, region-aware IDs). Adding it late is painful.

Everyday analogy. One shop open with a closed branch ready to open (active-passive), versus two branches both serving customers but needing to agree on stock numbers (active-active).

Common interview traps.

  • Saying active-active gives free availability. It brings conflict and consistency issues.
  • Forgetting the capacity math for losing a region.
  • Ignoring cross-region latency in synchronous replication.

notes.title: Replication, backups and point-in-time recovery
notes.html:
Replication keeps a live copy; backups keep history. You need both.

Replication modes:

  • Synchronous: the commit waits for the replica: RPO 0, but write latency includes the network RTT and availability depends on the replica. Cross-zone fine (1 to 2 ms), cross-region rarely (tens of ms per commit).
  • Asynchronous: the commit returns immediately; replica lags by milliseconds to seconds: RPO equals the lag at failure time (non-zero).
  • Semi-synchronous / quorum commit: at least one (or k of n) replica acks (Postgres synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (s1, s2)', MySQL semi-sync).
Postgres quorum commit (conceptual config)
synchronous_commit = on
synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (standby_az2, standby_az3)'
# Commit waits until any 1 standby has flushed WAL -> RPO ~0 inside the region, survives 1 standby loss

Point-in-time recovery (PITR). Take a base backup (e.g. daily) and continuously archive the write-ahead log (WAL) to object storage (S3). To recover to 10:42:17 (just before a bad DELETE), restore the base backup and replay WAL up to that time. RPO is about the WAL archive interval (seconds with streaming archive). Tools: pgBackRest, WAL-G, Barman for Postgres; AWS RDS automated backups (PITR with 5-minute granularity, retention up to 35 days; confirm current limits); MySQL binlogs.

Backup hygiene (3-2-1 rule). 3 copies, on 2 different media/systems, 1 offsite (another region or account). Protect backups from deletion: S3 Object Lock / immutable backups against ransomware, separate AWS account, versioning. Test restores regularly: an untested backup is a hope, not a backup.

Worked example. 2 TB Postgres, daily base backup (full ~2 TB compressed to ~600 GB) plus incremental WAL ~50 GB/day. Restore: download 600 GB at 500 MB/s is 20 minutes, replay 24 h of WAL at maybe 100 MB/s to 200 MB/s is under 10 minutes. RTO about 45 minutes before verification.

Real incident pattern. GitLab (Jan 31, 2017): an engineer removed the wrong database directory during replication troubleshooting; pg_dump backups were silently failing, S3 backup bucket empty, Azure disk snapshots not enabled for the DB; they recovered from a 6-hour-old LVM snapshot, losing about 6 hours of data. Lesson: monitor backup success, test restores.

Decision gravity. Retention length and immutability are reversible policy choices; the failure to test restores is the silent risk. Encryption key management for backups is a one-way door: lose the key and the backup is useless.

Industry examples. Amazon RDS/Aurora (continuous backup to S3), Google Cloud SQL PITR, Cloud Spanner backups, Etsy and GitHub with xtrabackup/replicas.

Everyday analogy. A video recording of your desk plus the photo album: the photo (base backup) plus a minute-by-minute diary (WAL) lets you reconstruct the desk at any moment.

Common interview traps.

  • Relying on replicas as backups.
  • Backups in the same account/region as the primary (one compromised account deletes both).
  • Not knowing how long a full restore takes.

notes.title: Failover: detection, promotion and traffic shifting
notes.html:
Failover is the sequence: detect failure, decide, promote the standby, redirect traffic, and fence the old primary.

Steps and timing (illustrative managed-DB numbers):

  1. Detect: health checks with consecutive failures (e.g. 3 x 10 s = 30 s). Faster detection raises false positives.
  2. Decide: automatic (needs reliable quorum/witness to avoid split brain) or manual (a human approves for region-level events, to avoid flapping).
  3. Promote: the replica becomes writable; check replication lag; for async you may lose the last transactions (RPO > 0).
  4. Redirect: DNS update (TTL 60 s but caches ignore it), global load balancer, or a service-discovery change. Connection pools must reconnect and applications must retry safely.
  5. Fence the old primary: make sure it cannot accept writes if it comes back (STONITH, read-only mode, revoke IAM), otherwise split brain.
  6. Rebuild redundancy: add a new standby.

Typical durations. Same-region Multi-AZ managed DB failover: 60 to 120 s (RDS docs commonly cite 1 to 2 minutes; Aurora often 30 s or less). Cross-region promotion: minutes plus DNS propagation. Kubernetes pod failure: seconds. Whole region evacuation with traffic steering: 1 to 10 min.

Traffic steering tools. DNS (Route 53 health-checked failover/latency records), global anycast load balancers (Cloudflare, Google Cloud Global LB, AWS Global Accelerator, which avoids DNS caching delays), service mesh locality failover (Envoy).

Worked example. 5,000 writes/s on async replication with 200 ms lag at failure: about 1,000 transactions (5,000 x 0.2) may be lost, which is the real RPO. Mitigation: semi-sync for critical tables, or reconcile from the application's event log/Kafka after failover.

Pitfalls.

  • Failback is harder than failover. Returning to the original region requires reverse replication and another cutover; plan it, and do not rush.
  • Control plane dependency: if your failover tool lives in the failed region, you cannot fail over. Keep the control plane independent (static stability: pre-provisioned capacity, no API calls needed during failure).
  • Thundering herd after failover: cold caches and connection storms overload the new primary; use warm-up and connection rate limits.

Industry examples. AWS "static stability" guidance; Facebook's Oct 2021 outage (BGP and DNS withdrawal made internal tools and even the data-centre access unreachable: control plane tied to the same network); Patroni/repmgr for Postgres HA; Orchestrator for MySQL; GitHub's 2018 incident from failover with split-brain-like divergence.

Decision gravity. Automatic vs manual failover: automatic is faster but can flap or split-brain on partial failures; many companies automate zone-level failover and keep region failover as a manual, rehearsed decision. Reversible by config.

Everyday analogy. A relief pilot: detect the captain is unwell, confirm, hand over controls, tell the tower, and make sure the original captain doesn't also grab the controls.

Common interview traps.

  • Ignoring failback and fencing.
  • DNS failover assuming clients honour the TTL.
  • A failover plan that depends on the very region that failed.

notes.title: Failover drills and game days
notes.html:
An untested DR plan almost always fails. Practice it on purpose.

Levels of practice:

  1. Tabletop exercise: talk through a scenario ("us-east-1 is gone, what do we do?") to find missing owners, runbooks, access.
  2. Restore test: regularly restore a backup into a scratch environment, run checksums/queries, record the actual duration (this becomes your measured RTO).
  3. Game day: controlled failure in production-like or production (kill a zone, block the primary) with observers and a stop button.
  4. Continuous chaos: automated random failure injection (Chaos Monkey; Netflix's Chaos Kong simulated whole-region loss).
  5. Regional evacuation drills: periodically run production traffic entirely from one region (Facebook's "storm" drills, Netflix regional failovers), proving capacity and tooling.

Checklist for a drill:

  • Define success: e.g. RTO 30 min, RPO 1 min, error rate below 1%.
  • Pre-announce, set blast-radius and abort criteria; have a rollback.
  • Verify with dashboards (SLO burn), not feelings.
  • Capture timeline, then fix gaps: missing IAM, expired certs, undersized standby, stale runbook, hardcoded IPs.
  • Re-run until boring.

Worked example. First drill: restore a 1.5 TB database. Expected RTO 1 h; actual 3 h 20 min because the restore role lacked KMS decrypt rights (45 min lost), the instance type was smaller than prod (1 h lost), and the runbook was outdated. Three fixes later, the second drill completes in 55 minutes.

Industry examples. Netflix Chaos Monkey/Kong; Google DiRT (Disaster Recovery Testing) exercises; AWS Fault Injection Service; Amazon "GameDay" tradition; Gremlin; GitHub and Stripe run regular failover tests.

Decision gravity. Drills cost engineering time and carry small risk but are cheap compared to a real failure; making them routine (quarterly) is a cultural choice. Fully reversible.

Everyday analogy. Fire drills: you find out the exit is blocked while the building is not on fire.

Common interview traps.

  • Documenting an RTO that was never measured.
  • Running drills only in staging that differs from prod.
  • Drills with no abort condition or no learning follow-up.

notes.title: Multi-region data and consistency trade-offs
notes.html:
Distance costs time: light in fibre travels about 200 km per ms, so a US-East to EU-West round trip is about 70 to 80 ms in practice, and to Asia 150 to 250 ms. That is a floor you cannot engineer away.

Options when a write must be durable in two regions:

  • Synchronous cross-region commit: adds one RTT to every write (e.g. +80 ms). Spanner/CockroachDB do this for strong consistency in multi-region mode, with tricks like placing the leaseholder near the users.
  • Async replication: fast writes, but non-zero RPO and eventual consistency across regions.
  • Per-user home region: pick the region where each user's data lives; most requests are local and fast; only cross-region requests pay.

Consistency patterns:

  • Read-your-writes: after a user writes, route their next reads to the same region (session stickiness, or read from primary for N seconds).
  • Global unique IDs: include a region code or use Snowflake-style IDs; do not rely on auto-increment across regions.
  • Idempotent event processing: replicate events through Kafka MirrorMaker/Cluster Linking and make consumers idempotent because duplicates and reordering appear around failover.
  • Global tables/secondary indexes: accept eventual consistency and design the UI for it.

Data residency. GDPR and country laws can require that some data stays in a region. This favors geo-sharding and shapes DR (backups can only go to allowed regions).

Cost. Cross-region data transfer costs money (on AWS roughly 0.02 USD/GB between regions; confirm current price). Replicating 20 TB/month is about 400 USD, but chatty cross-region service calls can silently add up.

Worked example. Chat app with 50M users across US/EU/Asia. Messages are stored in the sender's home region and replicated asynchronously to the recipient's region; delivery adds typically 100 to 300 ms inter-region latency, acceptable. Account creation uses a globally unique handle check: a rare strongly consistent global operation, done synchronously in a single "directory" region.

Industry examples. WhatsApp and Slack use regional/cell designs; Discord and Instagram use geo-aware routing; CockroachDB REGIONAL BY ROW; DynamoDB global tables; Cosmos DB multi-region with tunable consistency levels.

Decision gravity. Where each piece of data lives (home region, global, replicated) is a one-way door: re-homing data later is a migration project. Decide what MUST be strongly consistent globally (usernames, payments, inventory) and keep that set tiny.

Everyday analogy. Letters between cities: you can wait for confirmation of receipt every time (slow, certain), or send many and reconcile later (fast, occasionally confused).

Common interview traps.

  • Pretending cross-region synchronous replication is free.
  • Auto-increment IDs in multiple active regions.
  • Forgetting data residency law.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• RPO = data loss tolerance, RTO = downtime tolerance; each step lower costs roughly 10x. HA is not DR is not backup.
  • Four strategies: backup/restore, pilot light, warm standby, active-active; choose by business cost of downtime; moving to active-active later is a one-way door.
  • Active-active needs a data plan: home-region sharding, multi-leader conflict resolution, or cross-region consensus (Spanner, CockroachDB). Capacity must cover a lost region.
  • Replication (sync/async/quorum) does not replace backups; use PITR (base backup plus WAL), 3-2-1, immutable and offsite copies, and test restores (GitLab 2017).
  • Failover: detect, decide, promote, redirect, fence; failback is harder; keep the control plane independent of the failed region.
  • Drill regularly (tabletop, restore tests, game days, chaos); measure real RTO/RPO.
  • Cross-region latency (about 70 to 250 ms) is physics; keep strongly consistent global data minimal.
